" alt= " Sisters Lyhnix Baytops , 5 , left , and Aubri Baytops , 8 , right , draw on the sidewalk with chalk after school Thursday , Feb. 22 , 2018 , in Roanoke , Va . After someone gave his daughter some calcium sulphate sidewalk chalk , Joe Schwarcz found it yielded better results on the blackboard than the calcium carbonate chalk he had been using . " data-portal-copyright= " ERICA YOON " **28;134870;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1667877 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;134900;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; My first encounter with calcium sulphate was when I broke an ankle , way , way back in Grade 8 . I had no idea of the chemistry going on when the gauze bandages impregnated with some white stuff were wrapped around my ankle , hardening into a cast . Later , I would learn that the &amp;ldquo ; white stuff&amp;rdquo ; was &amp;ldquo ; Plaster of Paris&amp;rdquo ; or in chemical parlance , &amp;ldquo ; calcium sulphate hemihydrate. &amp;rdquo ; When moistened , Plaster of Paris is easily shaped , but hardens into a light-weight mass as it absorbs water and forms calcium sulphate dihydrate , better known as &amp;ldquo ; gypsum. &amp;rdquo ; Plaster of Paris is actually &amp;ldquo ; anhydrous calcium sulphate , &amp;rdquo ; prepared by heating gypsum to drive off water . It derives its name from the discovery of large deposits of gypsum in the Montmartre region of Paris in the 18th century . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; I bumped into calcium sulphate again in the undergraduate chemistry lab where we used the anhydrous version as a &amp;ldquo ; desiccant&amp;rdquo ; to dry chemicals that we had synthesized by placing them in a &amp;ldquo ; desiccator , &amp;rdquo ; a glass container with a tight-fitting lid and a desiccant at the bottom to absorb moisture . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Once I started teaching , I would have yet another meeting with calcium sulphate . That would be on the blackboard . Organic chemistry involves drawing numerous molecular structures , and back in the days before PowerPoint , the blackboard was the way to go . I had been inspired to work on my blackboard technique after attending a lecture by Robert Woodward , Harvard professor and Nobel laureate , who was renowned for his syntheses of extremely complex molecules as well as his blackboard skills . I practised and practised , but whereas Woodward&amp;rsquo ; s chalk had seemed to glide over the board , mine sputtered with stops and starts . Furthermore , his lines were broad and impactive , mine were squiggly . Then one day , lightning struck . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At my daughter&amp;rsquo ; s birthday party , she got a present , a box of sidewalk chalk . I wasn&amp;rsquo ; t thrilled by the potential consequences of this present and said that I would hang on to it until she was older . But when I picked up a piece of the chalk , it didn&amp;rsquo ; t feel like the one that I had been using . It was much softer , and thicker . Could my blackboard problems have been due to using the wrong type of chalk ? A little investigation revealed that chalk could be made of calcium carbonate or calcium sulphate . It wasn&amp;rsquo ; t hard to distinguish between the two . A few drops of hydrochloric acid applied to my chalk quickly resulted in the formation of bubbles of carbon dioxide indicating that it was made of calcium carbonate . I quickly purchased some calcium sulphate blackboard chalk . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; What a difference ! It practically floated across the board , leaving behind nice broad lines . I never went back to the carbonate again ! However , there was a downside to the change . When I had lectured about antacids , I always described how some of the most common ones were composed of calcium carbonate , since as a base , it was capable of neutralizing stomach acid . For emphasis , I would take a bite out my chalk . I couldn&amp;rsquo ; t do that with calcium sulphate since it does not neutralize acids . In the coming years , many students would eventually tell me that the lecture they remembered most was when their crazy professor ate chalk ! &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; I was happy with my calcium sulphate chalk , although it did break easily and produced more dust than I liked . Only recently did I come to learn that I could have done better . I could have gone for the Rolls Royce of chalks , the one that mathematicians have described as the &amp;ldquo ; nectar of the gods , &amp;rdquo ; one that melts like butter when you start writing . That is the &amp;ldquo ; Hagoromo Fulltouch Chalk , &amp;rdquo ; made by Hagoromo Bungu , a Japanese company . It seems this company had a process for formulating calcium carbonate into a soft chalk that was then coated with a waxy layer preventing it from breaking or giving off too much dust . Alas , the company stopped production in 2015 saying that blackboards had gone out of fashion , giving way to whiteboards and &amp;ldquo ; smart&amp;rdquo ; boards . At this devastating news , mathematicians started to buy up all available supplies and hoarded the chalk . Hagoromo&amp;rsquo ; s equipment was eventually sold to a Korean company that now again markets the &amp;ldquo ; umami of chalk . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; However , some claim that it is not as good as the original , a very limited supply of which is available from Amazon at $849 for 72 pieces . That&amp;rsquo ; s crazy , but the new version is available for $49.50 . Of course , I had to get it . It is not quite as good as my old calcium sulphate chalk , but it allowed me to eat chalk once more , although I&amp;rsquo ; m not that fond of the waxy coating . But then to my surprise , I discovered that a number of companies make &amp;ldquo ; edible chalk&amp;rdquo ; sourced from deposits in Ukraine . Got some . As it turns out , it also performs well on the blackboard . Life is good . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **29;134936;TOOLONG " **36;134967;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;Joe Schwarcz is director of McGill University 's Office for Science &amp; Society ( mcgill.ca/oss ) . He hosts The Dr. Joe Show on CJAD Radio 800 AM every Sunday from 3 to 4 p.m. &lt;/em&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt; &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;135005;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;135047;TOOLONG ... columns by Joe **29;135082;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; Joe Schwarcz , Special to the Montreal GazetteFri , 13 Dec 2019 16:41:13 **45;135113;TOOLONG ... Right Chemistry : Where things stand with omega-3 supplementshttp : **29;135160;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **33;135191;TOOLONG ... title= " " The scientific literature on omega-3 supplements is vast , and as is so often the case , can be cherry-picked to show either that they have great health benefits or that they are useless , " Joe Schwarcz writes . " alt= " " The scientific literature on omega-3 supplements is vast , and as is so often the case , can be cherry-picked to show either that they have great health benefits or that they are useless , " Joe Schwarcz writes . " data-portal-copyright= " Postmedia files " **28;135226;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1661442 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;135256;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; I do get some curious questions . &amp;ldquo ; Are there any fish parts used in Omega watches ? &amp;rdquo ; It wasn&amp;rsquo ; t difficult to guess that the question was prompted by the association of &amp;ldquo ; Omega&amp;rdquo ; with fish since the &amp;ldquo ; omega-3 fats&amp;rdquo ; found in fish oil have received a great deal of media attention due to their supposed health benefits . Since &amp;ldquo ; omega&amp;rdquo ; is the last letter in the Greek alphabet , the term , in this case , is used to denote &amp;ldquo ; the end&amp;rdquo ; of the chain of carbon atoms that make up a fatty acid . The number three refers to the presence of a carbon-carbon double bond on the third carbon from the end . No such fats , or any other fish parts , are used in Omega watches . The name likely was coined to suggest that as far as watches go , this was the ultimate , &amp;ldquo ; the end . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; I don&amp;rsquo ; t have an Omega watch , but I do have an interest in omega-3 fats because I have a fish allergy , meaning that fish oils are not part of my diet . So , I have wondered about taking &amp;ldquo ; fish oil&amp;rdquo ; supplements , sourced not from fish but from algae , which after all is where fish get them from . The scientific literature on omega-3 supplements is vast , and as is so often the case , can be cherry-picked to show either that they have great health benefits or that they are useless . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The stage for the fish oil controversy was set in 1971 by Danish researchers Hans Olaf Bang and Jorn Dyerberg who reported in The Lancet , a prime medical journal , their finding of low cholesterol and low triglyceride levels in the blood of Inuit living in Greenland . They used the term &amp;ldquo ; Eskimo , &amp;rdquo ; mentioning that the name derives from a native word meaning &amp;ldquo ; people eating raw meat . &amp;rdquo ; That etiology is controversial , and since &amp;ldquo ; Eskimo&amp;rdquo ; is considered by some to be offensive , the preferred expression is &amp;ldquo ; Inuit . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Finding low levels of cholesterol and triglycerides was surprising given that the Inuit diet was based mostly on animal products , which other studies had linked to high blood levels of the same substances . Bang and Dyerberg suggested that the difference was due to the type of animal fat consumed , which in the case of the Inuit came mostly from fish , seals and whales . These fats fall into the &amp;ldquo ; **25;135292;TOOLONG ; category and have different biochemical effects than the &amp;ldquo ; saturated&amp;rdquo ; fats in land-based animals . The authors of the Lancet paper also noted that the heart disease rate among the Inuit was much lower than among the general Danish population and hypothesized that this may be due to some protective effect offered by the marine fats . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Correctly , they clearly pointed out that such an observational study was not capable of proving a cause and effect relationship because other lifestyle factors may be involved . Perhaps it was the activity level of the Inuit that was protective , or maybe it wasn&amp;rsquo ; t what they were eating , but rather what they were not eating , namely the hamburgers , steaks , pizzas and processed staples of a western diet . Genetics did not appear to play a role . The Inuit living in Denmark had blood chemistries comparable to the rest of the Danish population . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some have criticized Bang and Dyberg , saying that their claim of fish fats offering protection against heart disease is not justified because they based their conclusion on unreliable reporting of the incidence of heart disease in Greenland . But the researchers never claimed that they had proven any such link , they just suggested that their study could be a springboard for randomized controlled trials using omega-3 supplements . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Indeed , there have been a number of such trials , the best of which were evaluated in a &amp;ldquo ; meta-analysis , &amp;rdquo ; essentially a study of studies , published in 2018 in the Journal of the American Medical Association . This included 10 randomized trials that involved at least 500 participants and a treatment duration of at least a year with various doses of supplements . The authors concluded that &amp;ldquo ; omega-3 fatty acids had no significant association with fatal or nonfatal coronary heart disease or any major vascular events . &amp;rdquo ; Case closed ? Nope . It never is. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 2019 , the results of a highly anticipated randomized , placebo-controlled trial involving more than 25,000 healthy participants taking one gram of omega-3 supplements a day for five years were published in the New England Journal of Medicine . While supplement takers did not have a lower incidence of total cardiovascular events , there was a reduced incidence of heart attacks , especially among people who do not eat fish . Another paper published in the same journal reported on a study in which subjects , who already had cardiovascular disease or diabetes , were supplemented with four grams of eicosapentaenoic acid ( EPA ) , a specific omega-3 fat . They had a 25 per cent reduced risk of cardiac events ! &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Frankly , given that studies have used different doses of supplements , different compositions and had different subject profiles , it is not possible to come to a firm conclusion about the potential benefits of supplements , although the evidence seems to be slightly in favour . But which one and how much ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There is better data on the Omega watch . It was worn by President John F. Kennedy at his inauguration , James Bond wore it in several films , and it was selected by NASA astronauts to be the first watch to go to the moon ! And that is no fish tale . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **29;135319;TOOLONG " **36;135350;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;Joe Schwarcz is director of McGill University 's Office for Science &amp; Society ( mcgill.ca/oss ) . He hosts The Dr. Joe Show on CJAD Radio 800 AM every Sunday from 3 to 4 p.m. &lt;/em&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt; &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;135388;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;135430;TOOLONG ... columns by Joe **29;135465;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; Joe Schwarcz , Special to the Montreal GazetteFri , 06 Dec 2019 11:00:34 **45;135496;TOOLONG ... Right Chemistry : Spy helped Soviets with polonium productionhttp : **30;135543;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **33;135575;TOOLONG ... title= " Russian President Vladimir Putin , right , listens to President of National Research Center " Kurchatov Institute " Mikhail Kovalchuk , as he visits Kurchatov Insitute of Atomic Energy , the home of the Soviet nuclear weapons program and later Soviet and Russian non-military nuclear technologies in Moscow , Russia , Tuesday , April 10 , 2018 . Back in the 1940s , the Soviets developed a nuclear bomb much sooner than the Americans had expected after an American spy working for Moscow shared vital information . " alt= " Russian President Vladimir Putin , right , listens to President of National Research Center " Kurchatov Institute " Mikhail Kovalchuk , as he visits Kurchatov Insitute of Atomic Energy , the home of the Soviet nuclear weapons program and later Soviet and Russian non-military nuclear technologies in Moscow , Russia , Tuesday , April 10 , 2018 . Back in the 1940s , the Soviets developed a nuclear bomb much sooner than the Americans had expected after an American spy working for Moscow shared vital information . " data-portal-copyright= " Alexei Nikolsky " **28;135610;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1654699 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;135640;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; Vladimir Putin strode to the podium in 2007 and announced that George Koval would be honoured with the prestigious gold star as a &amp;ldquo ; Hero of the Russian Federation . &amp;rdquo ; The proclamation was especially noteworthy given that Koval , who had died the year before at age 92 , was an American . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; What does it take for an American to become a Russian hero ? Providing critical information needed to construct an atomic bomb will do it . George Koval , you see , was a Soviet spy . &amp;ldquo ; Mr. Koval , &amp;rdquo ; President Putin stated , &amp;ldquo ; operated under the pseudonym Delmar and provided information that helped speed up the time it took for the Soviet Union to develop an atomic bomb of its own . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Koval was born to Russian immigrant parents in Iowa , but as an adult spent time in the Soviet Union , where he was recruited by military intelligence and trained as a spy before returning to the United States in 1940 . There he joined the army and by 1944 managed to secure a position as a &amp;ldquo ; health physics officer&amp;rdquo ; working at the Oak Ridge laboratories in Tennessee where as part of the Manhattan Project researchers were bombarding the nuclei of plutonium and uranium atoms with neutrons . The energy released when these nuclei were split into smaller fragments , or &amp;ldquo ; fissioned , &amp;rdquo ; was the key to developing the atom bomb . Koval began reporting on these activities to his &amp;ldquo ; handler , &amp;rdquo ; however his opportunity to make a real contribution to the Soviet nuclear program came in 1944 when he was transferred to a top secret lab in Dayton , Ohio . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It was there that critical work was being pursued to develop an &amp;ldquo ; initiator&amp;rdquo ; for fission reactions . Once a fission reaction begins , it generates neutrons that then trigger a &amp;ldquo ; chain reaction , &amp;rdquo ; but a source of neutrons is needed to initiate fission . These can be produced by bombarding beryllium with &amp;ldquo ; alpha particles&amp;rdquo ; emitted by polonium-210 , a naturally radioactive isotope . Alpha particles are composed of two protons and two neutrons and can act like minuscule bullets , in this case knocking out neutrons when they strike the nuclei of beryllium atoms . The problem was to secure a supply of polonium , a very rare element . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Back in 1898 , Marie and Pierre Curie had processed tons of an uranium ore known as pitchblende to finally isolate a few micrograms of a residue that had much greater radioactivity than could be accounted for by uranium . They surmised that the residue must contain a novel element . Marie , who incidentally coined the term &amp;ldquo ; radioactive , &amp;rdquo ; suggested that the newly discovered element be named polonium after her country of birth . To produce an &amp;ldquo ; initiator&amp;rdquo ; for the bomb , a more efficient way of procuring polonium had to be found . This was the task to be undertaken by the Dayton Project . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 1942 , Brigadier General Leslie Groves Jr. , director of the Manhattan Project , had approached the Monsanto chemical company to oversee the purification process needed to produce plutonium . Charles Allen Thomas , who later was to become president of Monsanto , was put in charge of the project . When the need for a polonium initiator became clear , he was also asked to find an efficient method of production . The research was carried out at Monsanto&amp;rsquo ; s labs in Dayton with a focus on isolating the desired polonium from lead oxide ore in which it occurs naturally , albeit in very small amounts . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As chemists were struggling to isolate polonium from the lead ore , a more ready supply became available . The Manhattan Project had developed a nuclear reactor capable of bombarding bismuth with neutrons to produce the desired isotope of polonium . Now the task was to separate the polonium from residual bismuth . This was soon mastered , allowing enough polonium to be produced for both the uranium bomb that was dropped on Hiroshima and the plutonium bomb that annihilated Nagasaki . It was the method production in Dayton of the initiator that Koval transmitted to the Soviets that resulted in their developing a nuclear bomb much sooner than the Americans had expected . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The alpha particles emitted by Polonium-210 can also target human tissues , causing severe damage . Indeed , polonium is one of the most toxic substances known . Ingesting or inhaling just a few micrograms can be lethal as evidenced by the celebrated poisoning in 2006 of former Soviet secret service agent Alexander Litvinenko in London . Litvinenko had sought asylum in Britain after being charged with exceeding the authority of his position in Russia . He had specialized in tackling organized crime and had run afoul of the authorities with his claim that the Russian government was involved in state-sponsored terrorism . In England he had authored two books that were highly critical of Russia , including accusing Vladimir Putin of ordering assassinations. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A British government investigation concluded that Litvinenko was likely poisoned by a Russian agent , probably by slipping polonium citrate or nitrate into his tea . A key was finding a radioactive tea kettle in Litvinenko&amp;rsquo ; s hotel room . The motive ? Litvinenko&amp;rsquo ; s revelations about Putin&amp;rsquo ; s links with the underworld . It goes without saying that Litvinenko will not be getting a gold star as a &amp;ldquo ; Hero of the Russian Federation . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **29;135676;TOOLONG " **36;135707;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;Joe Schwarcz is director of McGill University 's Office for Science &amp; Society ( mcgill.ca/oss ) . He hosts The Dr. Joe Show on CJAD Radio 800 AM every Sunday from 3 to 4 p.m. &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;135745;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;135787;TOOLONG ... columns by Joe **29;135822;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt; &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Joe Schwarcz , Special to the Montreal GazetteFri , 29 Nov 2019 16:30:11 **45;135853;TOOLONG ... Labos : Apple Watch is n't great as a medical devicehttp : **34;135900;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **33;135936;TOOLONG ... title= " An Apple Store employee shows the new Series 5 Apple Watch during the preview of the redesigned and reimagined Apple Fifth Avenue store in New York , U.S. , September 19 , 2019. " alt= " An Apple Store employee shows the new Series 5 Apple Watch during the preview of the redesigned and reimagined Apple Fifth Avenue store in New York , U.S. , September 19 , 2019. " data-portal-copyright= " Brendan McDermid " **28;135971;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1655635 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;136001;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; Apple wants to get into health care and they&amp;rsquo ; re betting heavily on their new Apple Watch . Previous versions , though , were a bit underwhelming . As I wrote &lt;a href= " https : **33;136037;TOOLONG ... a column last year , &lt;/a&gt; the Apple Watch 3 generated a lot of false positives for heart arrhythmias . But the latest version is supposed to be an upgrade , and the newly published &lt;a href= " https : **33;136072;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;Apple Heart Study&lt;/a&gt; was supposed to show off just how good the new and improved Apple Watch actually is at measuring your heart health . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The study was a massive undertaking . It enrolled more than 400,000 patients by using a downloadable app. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But the scale of the study obscures some downsides . Because patients had to already have their own Apple Watch and had to download the app to participate and record the data , the patient population skewed toward the young , the wealthy and the healthy . In the study , more than half of the participants were under 40 and only 6 per cent were over age 65. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As a result , very few patients actually had an irregular heartbeat during the trial . Only half of one per cent ended up receiving an alert from their watch . Sadly , most people seem to have ignored these results . The study protocol required people to go get a proper heart monitor ( in this case an ECG patch they would wear for seven days to determine whether they actually had an arrhythmia ) . But only about one in five people who got an alert from their phone actually complied . In the end , only 450 people submitted their ECG patches for analysis , which makes the Apple Heart Study fairly small by most measures . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In most cases the ECG patches did not find any arrhythmias ; they only diagnosed atrial fibrillation 35 per cent of the time . For people under 40 , who made up the majority of test subjects , the yield was only 18 per cent . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Atrial fibrillation is a very common type of arrhythmia whose main medical complication is an increased risk of stroke . Patients with atrial fibrillation who are over the age of 65 , or who have diabetes , high blood pressure , heart failure or a previous stroke would generally be given blood thinners as a preventative measure . However , most people would only give someone a diagnosis of atrial fibrillation if the arrhythmia lasted for more than 30 seconds . What to do with people who have brief episodes that last only a few seconds is less clear . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The problem with the Apple Watch is that it seems like it&amp;rsquo ; s going to generate many false positives . Many people will go for further testing only to be told either that their tests were normal or they were found to have short bouts of atrial fibrillation that do not require any treatment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There is a great deal of enthusiasm for medical technology and people naturally assume that newer better technology will inevitably lead to better health outcomes . But sometimes more sophisticated technology simply becomes better at diagnosing minor , ultimately inconsequential , issues that probably could have been ignored . The irony is that the Apple Watch is more common with young people where its detection rate is lower and where , even if atrial fibrillation were diagnosed , it is likely that blood thinners would not be prescribed to these young otherwise healthy patients with no risk factors . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As with any new technology , its effectiveness is based on how we use it . When used properly , testing for and treating atrial fibrillation is a very good way to prevent strokes in high-risk individuals . But screening everyone in the population is going to be an expensive low-yield activity . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Apple Watch is an incredible piece of technology . It just doesn&amp;rsquo ; t necessarily perform too well as a medical device , at least for now . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;Christopher Labos&lt;/em&gt; &lt;em&gt; is a Montreal doctor and an associate with the McGill Office for Science and Society . He also co-hosts a podcast called The Body of Evidence . &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Christopher Labos , Special to Montreal GazetteTue , 26 Nov 2019 20:35:24 **45;136107;TOOLONG ... &amp;amp ; FitnessOpinionPersonal TechThe Right Chemistry : A tarantula bite wo n't make you dancehttp : **35;136154;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **33;136191;TOOLONG ... title= " Zookeeper Jamie Mitchell poses for a photograph with a Mexican red-kneed tarantula during the annual stocktake of animals at ZSL London Zoo on January 4 , 2016 in London , England . " alt= " Zookeeper Jamie Mitchell poses for a photograph with a Mexican red-kneed tarantula during the annual stocktake of animals at ZSL London Zoo on January 4 , 2016 in London , England . " data-portal-copyright= " Carl Court " **28;136226;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1648128 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;136256;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;U&lt;/span&gt; ndoubtedly , being bitten by a tarantula is not a pleasant experience . Yet while it may cause some pain , it isn&amp;rsquo ; t going to cause the victim to go into a dancing frenzy . Unless the victim believes that it will ! That is just what happened in episodes of &amp;ldquo ; tarantism&amp;rdquo ; that broke out on a number of occasions between the 11th and 18th centuries in the province of Taranto in southern Italy . People who believed that they had been bitten by a type of spider , also named after &amp;ldquo ; Taranto , &amp;rdquo ; began to dance hysterically until they were &amp;ldquo ; cured&amp;rdquo ; by a special type of music with an upbeat tempo , usually featuring a tambourine . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The most curious aspect of tarantism is that there is no evidence the folks affected had actually been bitten , and of course , even if they had , the result would not be a frantic dance . Even if it were , it would not be cured by music . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Tarantism was actually an example of what has been called &amp;ldquo ; mass psychogenic illness . &amp;rdquo ; This occurs when large groups of people become sick because they believe that something has happened to make them sick , even though there is no actual causative agent . It is a stunning example of how the mind can rule the body . The &amp;ldquo ; tarantella&amp;rdquo ; is an Italian folk dance still performed today , the origins of which trace back to the tarantism of the Middle Ages . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Middle Ages also featured other examples of mass psychogenic illness , with the most famous one being the &amp;ldquo ; Dancing Plague of 1518&amp;rdquo ; that broke out in what is now the French city of Strasbourg . For some unknown reason , a single woman , &amp;ldquo ; Frau Troffea , &amp;rdquo ; began to dance fervently in the street and was soon joined by about 400 others who frolicked for days without rest until they collapsed from exhaustion . According to some reports , there were even deaths . One theory is that the bizarre behaviour was caused by eating grains contaminated with ergotamine , a psychoactive compound produced by the ergot fungus . An unlikely explanation since it supposes that all those involved ate contaminated grains and that they would all react the same way . It is far more likely that this was mass psychogenic illness induced by the stress of a miserable life . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; More recently , in 1998 , a high school teacher in the United States noted a &amp;ldquo ; gasoline-like&amp;rdquo ; smell in her classroom and told the students that she was experiencing a headache and was feeling nauseous , dizzy and short of breath . Soon a number of students in the classroom began to experience similar symptoms . As the classroom was being evacuated , a number of other students and staff began to complain of similar symptoms and sought medical care . After extensive investigation of blood , air and water samples by numerous government agencies , no toxins that could explain the symptoms were found . Authorities concluded that this was a case of mass psychogenic illness . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Another example of this phenomenon may be a condition now being called &amp;ldquo ; Idiopathic Environmental Intolerance attributed to Electromagnetic Fields . &amp;rdquo ; Victims claim they experience an assortment of headaches , fatigue , nausea , vertigo , difficulty concentrating , palpitations , tingling sensations , confusion , depression and indigestion that they attribute to electromagnetic radiation from cell phones , Wi-Fi routers or other electrical equipment . Since these people are undoubtedly suffering , there is an impetus to get to the bottom of the problem . There have now been some 46 trials in which sufferers were asked to determine if they were being exposed to real or sham electromagnetic fields in a blinded fashion . Despite the conviction of those afflicted , these trials have been unable the replicate the claim of electromagnetic sensitivity under controlled conditions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The researchers who analyzed all the available studies concluded that the most likely explanation for the symptoms is the &amp;ldquo ; nocebo effect , &amp;rdquo ; in which negative expectations cause symptoms even when there is no physiological reason for the symptoms . The term nocebo comes from the Latin for &amp;ldquo ; I shall harm&amp;rdquo ; and is the evil cousin of the placebo effect , deriving from the Latin for &amp;ldquo ; I shall please . &amp;rdquo ; This also explains why about 20 per cent of patients taking a sugar pill in controlled trials of drugs report side effects . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In yet another fascinating case , a man presented in an emergency room saying he felt terribly ill and admitted to taking a whole bottle of pills after a fight with his girlfriend . His blood pressure was very low and his heartbeat rapid . Response to treatment was poor . What sort of pills had he taken , the doctors asked ? The despondent patient explained that he had been enrolled in a clinical trial for an experimental anti-depressant drug and had taken all the pills he had been given . A quick call to the researcher in charge of the trial revealed that the man had been in the placebo arm of the study ! When told that the pills he had swallowed contained nothing but sugar , his heart rate and blood pressure quickly returned to normal . As the poet John Milton astutely noted , &amp;ldquo ; the mind can make a heaven of hell and a hell of heaven . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **29;136292;TOOLONG " **36;136323;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;Joe Schwarcz is director of McGill University 's Office for Science &amp; Society ( mcgill.ca/oss ) . Right Chemistry : Elderberry extract may help with colds , fluhttp : **37;136516;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **33;136555;TOOLONG ... title= " The botanical name of the elderberry plant is Sambucus nigra , with " nigra " being Latin for black , since the berries of the elderberry shrub have a deep blue-black colour . Eating the raw berries can cause illness . " alt= " The botanical name of the elderberry plant is Sambucus nigra , with " nigra " being Latin for black , since the berries of the elderberry shrub have a deep blue-black colour . Eating the raw berries can cause illness . " data-portal-copyright= " Tyrel Featherstone " **28;136590;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1641398 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;136620;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; There were not many science books available back in the 1620s . Copernicus had already published his On the Revolution of the Heavenly Spheres in 1543 , but Galileo&amp;rsquo ; s Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems would not appear until 1632 , and Newton would not lay the foundations for modern physics with his theory of gravity in Principia for another six decades . However , Martin Blochwich , a young German physician , made a lasting mark with his Anatomia Sambuci , or in English , The Anatomy of the Elder , a 300-page tome dedicated to a single plant , the elderberry . The botanical name of this plant is Sambucus nigra , with &amp;ldquo ; nigra&amp;rdquo ; being Latin for black , since the berries of the elderberry shrub have a deep blue-black colour . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In remarkable detail , Blochwich described the botany of the plant as well as the various oils , syrups , ointments , juice and wine that could be produced from its berries . The most appealing part of the book was a discussion of the ailments these preparations were supposed to be able to treat . Most of these treatments , such as for tuberculosis , stomach problems , tumours and toothache , were based on folklore rather than fact , but as it eventually turned out , elderberry extracts may have some merit when it comes to such infectious diseases as influenza and the common cold . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 1995 , Israeli researchers carried out a placebo-controlled double-blind study that demonstrated significantly faster resolution of symptoms of influenza with a standardized elderberry extract . This was further corroborated by another such trial in Norway , this time treating 60 influenza patients with 15 ml elderberry syrup or placebo four times a day for five days . Symptoms were relieved four days earlier in the treatment group . Then in 2016 , a placebo-controlled trial investigated colds in air travellers , since the frequency of infection in this group is known to be higher due to confinement in an aircraft . The placebo group participants had a significantly longer duration of cold episode days . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Exactly how elderberries deliver the goods isn&amp;rsquo ; t clear , but researchers have speculated that flavonoids in extracts stimulate the immune system by enhancing the production of cytokines , special proteins that cells involved in immune reactions use for communication . There is also some evidence that elderberry extracts interfere with the activity of hemagglutinin , a protein found on the surface of the influenza virus that binds it to the cell that is being infected . This suggests that elderberry preparations may be able to prevent infection if taken before exposure to the virus and can also keep the virus from spreading if taken after infection has occurred , thereby reducing the duration of symptoms . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Unfortunately , &amp;ldquo ; natural health products&amp;rdquo ; are poorly regulated and in many cases , ingredients are mystical . There are numerous elderberry products available , and due to a lack of information about their composition , evaluation of potential efficacy is difficult . However , most studies that have documented positive results have used a standardized , proprietary extract that goes by the commercial name of Sambucol , originally developed by Israeli virologist Madeleine Mumcuoglu. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; While commercially available standardized elderberry extracts such as Sambucol are safe , the same can not be said for home preparations . The elderberry plant produces sambunigrin , a &amp;ldquo ; cyanogenic glycoside&amp;rdquo ; that can liberate cyanide when digested . Not enough to be lethal , but enough to cause nausea , vomiting , abdominal cramps and weakness . It is found mostly in the leaves , stem and roots of the plant , but also occurs in small amounts in the seeds of the berries . If the berries are cooked , as is the case for syrups , there is no concern because any cyanide that forms will be released into the air as hydrogen cyanide . However , if elderberry juice is made by just crushing the berries without taking care to remove leaves and twigs , there can be problems . Back in 1983 , eight people in California had to be hospitalized after drinking a juice made from wild elderberries and other parts of the plant that they had gathered . All recovered within a few days . Had the concoction been heated , the problems could have been avoided . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A Columbia University professor who teaches a class on contemporary civilization learned about elderberry toxicity the hard way . By her own account , she is a &amp;ldquo ; great believer in natural this and that , &amp;rdquo ; and instead of taking a flu shot , she relied on a tincture she concocted from elderberries that she had grown to protect herself from infection by the flu virus . She became ill and ended up sending an email to her students explaining why she had to cancel class . Again , had she heated her brew , there would have been no issue . Would it have protected her from the flu ? There just isn&amp;rsquo ; t enough evidence to say . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For protection , the flu vaccine is a far better bet , but should the flu or a cold strike , there is evidence that Sambucol can be of help in relieving symptoms . In any case , the Columbia professor hopefully learned the important lesson that &amp;ldquo ; natural&amp;rdquo ; does not equal &amp;ldquo ; safe . &amp;rdquo ; Her university offers some excellent courses in chemistry . Maybe she should enrol . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **29;136656;TOOLONG " **36;136687;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;Joe Schwarcz is director of McGill University 's Office for Science &amp; Society ( mcgill.ca/oss ) . NewsOpinionScienceThe Right Chemistry : The good and bad with what powers your phonehttp : **35;136880;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **33;136917;TOOLONG ... title= " Akira Yoshino holds a model of a lithium-ion battery during a news conference in Tokyo . Yoshino won the 2019 Nobel Prize in chemistry with John B. Goodenough and M. Stanley Whittingham . " alt= " Akira Yoshino holds a model of a lithium-ion battery during a news conference in Tokyo . Yoshino won the 2019 Nobel Prize in chemistry with John B. Goodenough and M. Stanley Whittingham . " data-portal-copyright= " Tomohiro Ohsumi " **28;136952;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1634670 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;136982;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;It is the lightest of all the solid elements , but it certainly is n't a lightweight when it comes to the punch it can pack . We are talking about lithium , an element whose compounds are at the heart of the lithium-ion batteries that power our cellphones , laptops and electric vehicles . Little wonder that the 2019 Nobel Prize in chemistry was awarded to professors John B. Goodenough , M. Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino for the development of such batteries . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;Lithium metal reacts readily with moisture and with oxygen so it is never found in its elemental state . For commercial production , lithium salts are extracted from water in mineral springs , brine pools or brine deposits found mostly in Chile and Australia and are subjected to an electric current that converts the lithium ions to metallic lithium . This can be used to produce the lithium cobalt oxide used in lithium-ion batteries . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;A typical lithium-ion battery consists of an electrode made of lithium cobalt oxide and another made of graphite , with the two separated by an electrolyte solution through which lithium ions can readily move . There is also a polyethylene barrier , just a few microns thick , that allows the passage of the lithium ions but is impervious to electrons , forcing these to travel through an external circuit . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;When charging , a power supply is connected to the electrodes sending a stream of electrons , that is a current , toward the graphite electrode which then becomes negatively charged with the electrons being trapped in the graphite . At the same time , electrons are withdrawn from the lithium cobalt oxide electrode that then releases positively charged lithium ions . These are attracted to the negative graphite electrode where they eventually become embedded . Since graphite is an insulator , the electrons and the lithium ions in the graphite are kept from combining . Now the cell is " charged . " &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;When it comes to discharge , instead of a power source , the electrodes are connected to whatever equipment is to be run on electricity . Now the lithium ions are attracted back toward the lithium cobalt oxide electrode whence they came because being locked into a stable matrix with other metals is a more stable arrangement . The electrons , unable to flow through the barrier between the electrodes , pass through the external circuit , generating a current . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;There is no question that lithium-ion batteries have changed the way the world functions . But as always , with any advancement , there is a " but . " In this case , there are issues about the environmental consequences of extraction of the necessary nickel , copper , lithium and cobalt from their ores , as well as about possible health effects when it comes to the workers involved . Then there is the problem of recycling as well as concerns about the batteries possibly igniting and causing fires . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;The extraction and processing of lithium has a large environmental footprint . It requires a great deal of water , loads of energy and emits greenhouse gases . Recycling is also becoming a bigger and bigger issue as spent batteries from vehicles pile up . Today , only about five per cent of batteries are recycled , with the rest ending up in landfills , potentially releasing metals that contaminate soil and groundwater . The barrier to recycling is the need for expensive , sophisticated equipment to treat harmful emissions , as well as the costs associated with the collection , storage and transport of spent batteries . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;Cobalt recycling is more critical than that of lithium since waste from cobalt mining pollutes water systems and has a number of health risks associated with it . Exposure to pulverized dust containing cobalt can cause contact dermatitis as well as respiratory sensitization , asthma , decreased pulmonary function and shortness of breath . Most cobalt is mined in the Congo where there is a lack of basic protective equipment such as face masks and gloves -- and because of poverty , child labour is common . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;Then there is fire . There are scary accounts of cellphones catching fire and airplanes crashing when lithium-ion batteries suddenly ignited . Keep in mind , though , that relative to the number of such batteries in use , the risk of fire is minute . It happens when a battery is short-circuited , usually by damage to the thin barrier that prevents electrons from flowing through the battery . If electrons do pass through , they generate a current that can ignite the pressurized , flammable electrolyte . That can occur if the battery is physically damaged , or if faulty manufacturing leaves behind tiny metal particles that are capable of causing a short circuit . Such flaws have resulted in recalls , such as some Samsung Galaxy phones . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;Research into improved batteries is intense and there is no doubt that advances are on the horizon both in efficiency and safety as well as in recycling technology . And now that I 'm finished typing on my lithium-ion battery powered laptop , I 'll make a few calls on my lithium-ion battery powered cellphone , including one to lithium-ion battery powered car manufacturers to ask about recycling . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **29;137018;TOOLONG " **36;137049;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;Joe Schwarcz is director of McGill University 's Office for Science &amp; Society ( mcgill.ca/oss ) . Hydro-Qu ? bec is preparing for the future -- and so should youhttp : **37;137605;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **33;137644;TOOLONG ... title= " Aerial view of Hydro-Qu ? bec 's Romaine 1 hydroelectric dam . The demand for power is increasing as we plug in more and more devices during peak use periods . " data-portal-copyright= " LARS HAGBERG " **28;137679;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1628675 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;137709;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;Hydro-Qu ? bec 's recent announcement of its new division , Hilo&lt;/a&gt; , which will offer customers new tools to reduce their energy consumption , went practically unnoticed . One reason might be that the company provided no details about what the tools will be . Yet there&amp;rsquo ; s an important story behind Hilo that all Hydro-Qu&amp;eacute ; bec customers should hear . Quebecers&amp;rsquo ; ability to reduce their energy needs will be a game changer in the energy transition , both here and across the northeastern part of the continent . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hilo&amp;rsquo ; s offerings will include intelligent thermometers and systems to control lights remotely from a computer or smartphone . Details about the full gamut of products are sketchy because the products are still in development . No one can foresee exactly what customers&amp;rsquo ; needs will be . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; However , Hydro-Qu&amp;eacute ; bec&amp;rsquo ; s immediate goal is clear &amp;mdash ; and urgent . Hilo was created to solve a pressing , chronic problem : Hydro-Qu&amp;eacute ; bec&amp;rsquo ; s shortage of power . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hydro-Qu&amp;eacute ; bec is in a paradoxical situation . On one hand , the company enjoys huge yearly surpluses of energy , up to 18 terawatt-hours . Yet the company increasingly faces shortages of power . Why ? Unlike energy , which is the total amount of electricity customers pay for at the end of the month , measured in kilowatt hours , power is the amount of energy required at a specific time , measured in kilowatts . Like everywhere else in the developed world , Quebecers&amp;rsquo ; overall energy needs have been stable since 2007 , mostly due to increased energy efficiency . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Yet the demand for power in Quebec is increasing by 100 or 200 megawatts per year . Hydro-Qu&amp;eacute ; bec predicts that by 2025 , it will be short 1,000 megawatts of power , or two-thirds of the output of the new Romaine hydro complex on the North Shore . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The reason power demand is increasing is simple : We plug in more and more devices during peak use periods . If Hydro-Qu&amp;eacute ; bec doesn&amp;rsquo ; t produce enough kilowatts to satisfy increasing requirements , the entire electrical system could fail . The power problem is all the more acute since the majority of Quebecers heat their homes with electricity . Electric cars could make power shortages more acute because customers will tend to plug their car in at the same time , after work . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the past , Hydro-Qu&amp;eacute ; bec would have simply built a new dam to meet increasing needs . Now it is opting for a cheaper , more environmental solution : spreading power use more evenly over the day . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hilo will offer bonuses to customers who shift their power use away from peak periods in the morning and evening to times when there is less overall demand , like the middle of the afternoon or even the middle of the night . It will be possible to charge your electric car automatically while you sleep , for example . Hilo is developing algorithms to co-ordinate heating houses among neighbours , so everyone isn&amp;rsquo ; t jacking the thermostat at the same time . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Officially , Hydro-Qu&amp;eacute ; bec has not announced how many megawatts of power it aims to save , but unofficially , leaders at the company say they hope to reduce consumption by 5,000 megawatts , or 12 per cent of Hydro&amp;rsquo ; s installed capacity . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; If Hilo takes off and power demand falls , Quebec won&amp;rsquo ; t have to buy extra power from its neighbours or build new dams . Instead , Hydro-Qu&amp;eacute ; bec will be able to store and export more energy to its neighbours . Hydro-Qu&amp;eacute ; bec already supplies four per cent of Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s electricity and 25 per cent of Vermont&amp;rsquo ; s . In 2016 and 2017 , Vermont , Massachusetts and New York state adopted specific measures to force their energy suppliers to include renewable energies in their offer . Hydro-Qu&amp;eacute ; bec could go a long way to meeting these needs . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Quebec&amp;rsquo ; s hydroelectricity , which is 99.8 per cent renewable , is the cheapest , greenest source of renewable energy on the continent . Everyone stands to gain if Quebecers learn to use it more wisely . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;&lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;Julie Barlow and Jean-Beno ? t Nadeau are the authors of Charging Ahead : Hydro-Qu ? bec and the Future of Electricity ( Baraka Books ) &lt;/span&gt;&lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;137744;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;137786;TOOLONG ... turn Hydro-Qu ? bec into a tax-collecting machine , business group **27;137821;TOOLONG &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;137850;TOOLONG ... poised to profit from U.S. thirst for green **27;137885;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; Julie Barlow and Jean-Beno ? t Nadeau , Special to Montreal GazetteTue , 29 Oct 2019 16:51:09 **45;137914;TOOLONG ... Right Chemistry : A magical connection between Houdini and Lincolnhttp : **33;137961;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **33;137996;TOOLONG ... title= " Harry Houdini was greatly perturbed by mediums who used tricks to defraud people and was a staunch foe of spiritualists. " alt= " Harry Houdini was greatly perturbed by mediums who used tricks to defraud people and was a staunch foe of spiritualists. " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;138031;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1619931 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;138061;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; One day in the early 1900s , Robert Todd Lincoln , son of the assassinated president , was surprised to receive a photograph from Harry Houdini , the most celebrated magician of the times . In the picture , Houdini is seen apparently conversing with &amp;ldquo ; Honest Abe . &amp;rdquo ; Since Lincoln was assassinated in 1865 and Houdini was born in 1874 , the only way they could have appeared together in a photo was if Lincoln&amp;rsquo ; s image was a manifestation of his &amp;ldquo ; spirit . &amp;rdquo ; Basically , the photo purported to show Houdini conversing with the ghost of the slain president ! &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Such spirit photos were quite the rage at the time . The Civil War had brought spiritualism to the forefront with distraught relatives of soldiers who perished in battle hoping to communicate with their spirits . Mediums capitalized on such folly by duping the gullible with photographs that were obviously taken after a soldier&amp;rsquo ; s death but nevertheless clearly showed their image , which was claimed to be a spirit apparition. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Houdini was greatly perturbed by mediums who used tricks to defraud people and was a staunch foe of spiritualists . Being a great admirer of President Lincoln , he was especially angered by mediums who claimed to have made contact with the late president and attacked them with vigour . When a medium professed to have spirit photographs of Lincoln , Houdini sent a photo of himself together with Lincoln to the president&amp;rsquo ; s son to ensure he would not be ensnared by the medium&amp;rsquo ; s chicanery . There was an accompanying explanation describing how such photos can be readily produced with double exposure techniques . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Houdini venerated Lincoln and was an enthusiastic collector of Lincoln memorabilia . Exactly why he had become so devoted to Lincoln&amp;rsquo ; s history isn&amp;rsquo ; t clear , but it may well have been due to the president&amp;rsquo ; s connection to escape artist and magician Horatio Cooke during the Civil War . At the age of 18 , Cooke joined the Union army and amazed his fellow soldiers with magic tricks and an uncanny ability to escape when tied up with ropes . Secretary of War Edwin Stanton came to hear about Cooke&amp;rsquo ; s prodigious feats and thought that they could be put to some use . He invited Cooke to demonstrate his talents at a meeting that much to the soldier&amp;rsquo ; s surprise included Lincoln . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Cooke was tied up with 50 feet of rope and quickly managed to liberate himself , a feat that so amazed the president that he appointed Cooke as a federal scout with a mission of penetrating Confederate lines as a spy and sending back reports of activities . Were he to be captured , the president thought , Cooke would have a good chance of escaping . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Indeed , he was captured and tied to a tree to be dealt with in the morning , which likely meant execution . But Cooke managed to put his talents to use , freed himself from the ropes and escaped . After the war he forged a career as a professional magician , calling himself &amp;ldquo ; Professor Harry Cooke . &amp;rdquo ; He also became fascinated with spiritualism and recognized that mediums were using various magic effects to convince sitters at a s&amp;eacute ; ance that spirits were present . Cooke was so disturbed by this that he began to bill himself as the &amp;ldquo ; Celebrated King of Spirit Exposers&amp;rdquo ; and devoted his performances to debunking spiritualists . His exposes were very effective and so enraged spiritualists that a believer shot Cooke at point blank range . He recovered and went on to perform for another quarter of a century . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Cooke&amp;rsquo ; s story appealed to Houdini because he had the same disdain for spiritualists and had often been threatened by them . He went out of his way to visit Cooke who had obtained the moniker &amp;ldquo ; The Oldest Living Magician&amp;rdquo ; in Los Angeles , and credited him in his 1924 book A Magician Among the Spirits for exposing the stealthy work of mediums . Cooke died that year but not before , at the age of 80 , in front of an assembly of magicians , wearing a Union uniform , he reprised the escape he had performed in front of Lincoln some 60 years earlier . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There is yet another reason for which Houdini held Lincoln in regard . He was keenly aware of a story about the president&amp;rsquo ; s interest in magic . At a rehearsal for a July 4 parade , a magician produced an egg from the mouth of the president&amp;rsquo ; s son , and upon being introduced to the magician , Lincoln surprised him by saying , &amp;ldquo ; Why of course , it&amp;rsquo ; s Signor Blitz , one of the most famous men in America . &amp;rdquo ; Lincoln knew that Blitz had performed at many Union Army Hospitals during the Civil War and was thankful for the magic he had brought to the soldiers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Now you know of the magical connection between Harry Houdini and the 16th president of the U.S. At his stage performances , Houdini paid homage to the president with an eagle that magically appeared out of a blend of red , white and blue streamers . The eagle&amp;rsquo ; s name ? &amp;ldquo ; Abe Lincoln . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **29;138097;TOOLONG " **36;138128;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;Joe Schwarcz is director of McGill University 's Office for Science &amp; Society ( mcgill.ca/oss ) . BusinessThe Right Chemistry : Looking for the secrets to longevityhttp : **31;138715;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **33;138748;TOOLONG ... title= " Some research suggests that the best way to slow aging might be to follow a low-calorie diet high in whole grains , fruits , vegetables , beans and fish . " alt= " Some research suggests that the best way to slow aging might be to follow a low-calorie diet high in whole grains , fruits , vegetables , beans and fish . " data-portal-copyright= " Justin Sullivan " **28;138783;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1612460 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;138813;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; We can&amp;rsquo ; t avoid aging . Every passing minute brings us one minute closer to the end . Not a pleasant thought . So , it is little wonder that the term &amp;ldquo ; anti-aging&amp;rdquo ; has been seized by marketers of various cosmetics , health supplements , exotic juices and dietary regimens. &amp;ldquo ; Anti-aging medicine&amp;rdquo ; is a growing field with numerous biotech companies working on drugs designed to combat the aging process . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The quest for immortality , of course , is not new . The ancient alchemists sought to turn base metals like lead into gold in order to find the secret of gold&amp;rsquo ; s &amp;ldquo ; immortality . &amp;rdquo ; After all , the metal would not tarnish , it maintained its beautiful sheen and seemed to last forever . If they could find its magic , they could perhaps apply it to humans . But they never did find the secret . Lead is still lead and the alchemists are long dead . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This is not to say that there are not some intriguing possibilities that may help slow down the clock . As we age , an increasing number of our cells enter a stage of &amp;ldquo ; senescence&amp;rdquo ; in which they no longer divide and begin to release chemicals that cause inflammation resulting in damage to tissues . A buildup of senescent cells , sometimes called &amp;ldquo ; zombie cells , &amp;rdquo ; is a hallmark of aging . Can anything be done to prevent this buildup ? Possibly . At least in mice . When researchers at the Mayo Clinic injected just a small number of senescent cells into young mice , their speed , endurance and strength eroded to that seen in a senior mouse in just a few weeks . When the mice were then treated with desatinib and quercetin , a combination of drugs known to destroy senescent cells , they recovered most of their lost physical capabilities within two weeks ! Quite dramatic ! But mice are not people , and while quercetin is a safe compound extracted from apple peel , desatinib is a very expensive leukemia drug with loads of side effects . Still , this experiment is a proof of principle , demonstrating that destroying senescent cells with &amp;ldquo ; senolytics&amp;rdquo ; is worthy of exploration . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; However , slowing aging may not be a matter of what we do , but what we don&amp;rsquo ; t do . It may be that if we want to live longer , all we have to do is eat less . Calorie restriction has been the only sure-fire way that scientists have found to slow aging in animals from rodents to monkeys and now we are beginning to accumulate data that suggests this applies to humans , as well . The idea that less is more when it comes to eating is not new . Hippocrates noted that fat people were more likely to die suddenly than slender ones , and Avicenna , the famed Persian philosopher and physician , suggested that the elderly should eat less than when they were younger . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Venetian nobleman Luigi Cornaro may have been the first to put a restricted calorie diet to a test in the 17th century when he came to believe that his health was deteriorating due to excessive partaking of food , drink and sex . He then restricted himself to no more than 350 grams of food a day and 400 mL of wine and lived to the ripe old age of 98 . He documented his regimen in his book Discourses On the Temperate Life and described how the changes he made in his lifestyle allowed him to remain in vigorous health well into old age . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Today , members of the Calorie Restriction Society that has the goal of increasing longevity are following in Cornaro&amp;rsquo ; s footsteps and are acting as human guinea pigs . They consume no more than 2,000 calories per day , which is just over half of what an average North American wolfs down . They don&amp;rsquo ; t do this , though , by eating half servings of hamburger , fries or pizza . They do it by following a diet high in whole grains , fruits , vegetables , beans and fish . And according to a study published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology , the austere regimen is paying off . Researchers examined the heart function of 25 members of the Calorie Restriction Society , and to their amazement found that the hearts functioned like those of people 15 years younger . But permanent hunger is not appealing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; What is appealing , however , is taking a deep dive into the science of aging . That is just what we will do this year at our annual Trottier Public Science Symposium , one of McGill&amp;rsquo ; s largest annual public events . We have invited three expert speakers to address humans&amp;rsquo ; &amp;ldquo ; Longing for Longevity . &amp;rdquo ; On Tuesday , Oct. 22 , Harvard Professor of Genetics David Sinclair , a world leader in aging research , will discuss how aging may be a treatable disease , and cosmetic chemist Kelly Dobos will scrutinize claims made by producers of anti-aging cosmetics . On Wednesday , Oct. 23 , Ruth Westheimer , psychosexual therapist , author and pioneer of radio and television programs dealing with sexual issues will speak on Sex After 50 . ( Spoiler : there is. ) &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The symposium will&amp;nbsp ; take place at 7 p.m. both days at the Centre Mont Royal , 1000 Sherbrooke St. West . Admission is free . " data-portal-copyright= " SEBASTIEN ST-JEAN " **28;139145;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1617163 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The environment and the climate have been central in this federal election campaign , but too often the discussions have been limited to pipelines and carbon taxes . While eliminating fossil subsidies and putting a price on carbon will no doubt foster lifestyle changes and push companies to adopt new procedures , they hardly measure up to the gigantic scope of what is required . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The challenge of transforming virtually our entire energy infrastructure in a mere 30 years is so colossal that it dwarfs the Manhattan Project or the Apollo moonshot . Such a rapid development of new technology &amp;mdash ; much of which hasn&amp;rsquo ; t even been invented &amp;mdash ; will require massive government investment in fundamental and applied science ; it will not occur merely by tweaking the tax system or by eating less meat . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Unfortunately , in spite of a series of low-cost , high-profile climate initiatives , the Trudeau government continued Harper&amp;rsquo ; s policy of disinvestment in science and innovation . The reality is that ever since last year&amp;rsquo ; s shutdown of the Climate Change and Atmospheric Research ( CCAR ) program , Canada has had a gaping climate science hole . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The sorry state of Canadian climate science was recently documented by the report &lt;a href= " https : **33;139175;TOOLONG ... in Canadian Climate Science&lt;/a&gt; , which , among other things , showed that over the previous decade , Canada&amp;rsquo ; s funding of atmospheric climate science was about half of comparable international levels and was microscopic compared to its fossil fuel subsidies or pipeline buyouts . Unsurprisingly , this lack of funding has contributed to a &lt;a href= " https : **33;139210;TOOLONG ... drain of climate scientists out of Canada . &lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Since the demise of the CCAR , the government appears to think that the only purpose of climate science is to make climate projections to the year 2050 or 2100 . Now that the technocrats are satisfied with the projections , they want the scientists to go home and let the economists , sociologists , psychologists , computer experts and communicators pick up the slack . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Without climate science and scientists , Canada&amp;rsquo ; s new initiatives can lead to ironic outcomes . In May , this was brought home to me when I was solicited to lend guidance to a &amp;ldquo ; climate awareness&amp;rdquo ; project under the auspices of another post CCAR initiative , the &lt;a href= " https : **33;139245;TOOLONG ... Action Fund&lt;/a&gt; ( CAF ) . The CAF targets &amp;ldquo ; students , youth , Indigenous peoples and organizations&amp;rdquo ; with the goal of raising &amp;ldquo ; awareness of climate change . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; I was approached by a team of computer scientists who were aware that my McGill group had developed qualitatively new methods to project the climate throughout the 21st century that were less uncertain than conventional approaches . The team was large &amp;mdash ; boasting six interns and three post-doctoral fellows &amp;mdash ; but their project nevertheless lacked climate science expertise . Their goal was to produce enhanced imagery of houses and neighbourhoods , projected throughout the 21st century according to different greenhouse gas emission scenarios . For example , they wanted to produce realistic films of houses and neighbourhoods during climate enhanced flooding events . It was hoped that images of a person&amp;rsquo ; s own home under a metre of water would elicit an emotional response that would lead to climate awareness where , until now , knowledge and rational discourse had failed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Unfortunately , projecting trends of future precipitation and floods is a largely unsolved scientific problem . It is very different from projecting future temperatures . While there is no doubt that temperatures will rise nearly everywhere , the situation for precipitation is not so clear . The overall total global amount of precipitation will certainly increase , but local uncertainties are so large that , for most areas , we don&amp;rsquo ; t yet know whether they will become wetter or drier . Precipitation is only one of the numerous climate science challenges that urgently require further research . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Science without awareness leads to inaction . I therefore accepted to voluntarily help guide the project . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Yet awareness without knowledge leads to despair . A better future will require not only awareness and knowledge ; it will require action . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;Shaun Lovejoy is a professor of physics at McGill University and a fellow of the American Geophysical Union . &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; Shaun Lovejoy , Special to Montreal GazetteThu , 17 Oct 2019 16:42:59 **45;139280;TOOLONG ... 2019OpinionScienceThe Right Chemistry : The opening of King Tutankhamen 's tombhttp : **36;139327;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **33;139365;TOOLONG ... title= " This file photo taken on November 28 , 2015 shows the sarcophagus of King Tutankhamun displayed in his burial chamber in the Valley of the Kings , close to Luxor , 500 kms south of the Egyptian capital , Cairo . " alt= " This file photo taken on November 28 , 2015 shows the sarcophagus of King Tutankhamun displayed in his burial chamber in the Valley of the Kings , close to Luxor , 500 kms south of the Egyptian capital , Cairo . " data-portal-copyright= " KHALED DESOUKI " **28;139400;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1608079 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **33;139430;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; Feb. 17 , 1923 marked one of the most important dates in the history of archeology . In the presence of 20 witnesses , archeologist Howard Carter unsealed an intact ancient Egyptian tomb he had discovered in the Valley of the Kings three months earlier . Eyes feasted on a throne covered in gold leaf , but it was a stone sarcophagus and its beautifully gilded inner coffins that would get the most attention . Inside was the mummy of &amp;ldquo ; the boy king&amp;rdquo ; Tutankhamen adorned with the magnificent gold mask that has since become famous around the world . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There were more than 5,000 other items found in the tomb including food , wine , archery bows and fresh linen underwear . It would not be fitting for the spirit of royalty to appear in the Hall of Judgement hungry , thirsty and sporting dirty garments . It was in that Hall that Osiris , the god of afterlife , lord of the dead and rebirth , assessed the purity of a person&amp;rsquo ; s heart . The Egyptians believed that the heart , not the brain , was the essence of a person and its &amp;ldquo ; purity&amp;rdquo ; reflected lifetime deeds . If the heart was judged to be pure , the spirit was allowed to enter immortal paradise . If not , the heart was forfeited to Ammit , the goddess who was the &amp;ldquo ; Devourer of the Dead&amp;rdquo ; and was ready to swallow the tainted heart thereby condemning the soul to a &amp;ldquo ; second death&amp;rdquo ; from which there was no escape . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Egyptians did not think that the body would literally come back to life ; after all , there was plenty of evidence that this did not happen . The curse of mummies wandering around with outstretched arms ready to torment the living was a creation of 20th-century filmmakers . What the Egyptians did believe was that the spirit had to regularly return to the body for sustenance , hence the importance of preserving the corpse through mummification . Funeral masks were placed over the deceased&amp;rsquo ; s face so that the spirit could recognize the body upon its return . Since the home of the spirit was the heart it was preserved and replaced in the body cavity . The unimportant brain was removed with special tools through the nose and discarded . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A variety of amulets , &amp;ldquo ; good luck charms&amp;rdquo ; that were blessed by priests with special incantations to offer protection against evil and unhappiness , were often included with the mummy . The most widely used amulets were replicas of &amp;ldquo ; scarab beetles , &amp;rdquo ; now commonly referred to as &amp;ldquo ; dung beetles . &amp;rdquo ; To the ancient Egyptians these insects were sacred because of their practice of collecting dung and rolling it into a ball . This seemed akin to the ritual followed by Khepri , the god who was believed to roll the sun across the sky every day , just like a dung beetle rolls dung . Indeed , Khepri was often represented as a scarab-headed man . The scarab was also seen as a symbol of rebirth and regeneration since it lays its eggs in the ball of dung from which its offspring eventually emerge . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Scarab replicas were carved out of stone or ivory , or formulated from an early form of ceramic made by mixing sand or crushed quartz with sodium carbonate ( soda ) and calcium oxide ( lime ) . When fired at a high temperature , this mixture vitrifies and develops a glaze on the surface that can take on a blue or green colour if copper compounds are incorporated into the mix . Scarabs were worn as necklaces , distributed around the home , and were also placed on the chest of a deceased person just over the heart to prevent any sins that had been accumulated in life from being released when Osiris weighed the heart for purity . Tutankhamen had a large scarab carved out of stone on his chest . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Just how the purity of Tutankhamen&amp;rsquo ; s heart may have been judged we will never know . Aside from some minor restorations of temples , he does not seem to have accomplished much in his young life , but then again , he was only on the throne for nine of his 17 years . On the other hand , there is no evidence that he would have done anything to defile the purity of his heart . While he didn&amp;rsquo ; t do much in life , in death Tutankhamen has become probably the most famous of the pharaohs . This is due partially to the golden mask that has been exhibited and admired around the world as well as the supposed curse that was inflicted on all who tampered with his tomb . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That curse , basically the invention of newspapers seeking publicity , supposedly resulted in the premature death of people who were in any way associated with the opening of the tomb . The fact is that of the 58 people who were present when the tomb and &lt;a href= " https : **25;139465;TOOLONG : //en. ... were opened , only eight died within a dozen years ; Howard Carter died of &lt;a href= " https : **25;139492;TOOLONG : //en. ... in 1939 at the age of 64 . There was nothing unusual about the deaths . There was no pharaoh&amp;rsquo ; s curse . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **29;139519;TOOLONG " **36;139550;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;Joe Schwarcz is director of McGill University 's Office for Science &amp; Society ( mcgill.ca/oss ) .
